summary: Market wrap for Thursday 5 October 2023: the ASX was set to open higher after Wall Street rebounded on weaker-than-expected US jobs and services data, which eased Treasury yields and sent oil down about 5.6 per cent. Energy and mining stocks lagged locally, while Dimerix doubled on a licensing deal. The note also covers Fed rate expectations, the ouster of Kevin McCarthy and the shutdown risk, and weak Christmas spending forecasts.
one_line: ASX poised to rise after Wall Street rebounded on cooling US data, lower bond yields and a sharp oil price fall.
key_facts: Melbourne-based biotech Dimerix more than doubled its share price to 16¢ after signing an exclusive licensing deal to commercialise its Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis kidney disease treatment in Europe, the UK, Switzerland, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.
Energy companies fell 0.9 per cent on the ASX as oil slumped; Woodside fell 0.8 per cent, Santos 0.4 per cent and Ampol 2.8 per cent.
Iron ore fell 1.1 per cent, pulling Rio Tinto down 1.5 per cent and BHP down 0.7 per cent; IGO fell 4 per cent and Mineral Resources 2.9 per cent.
Aristocrat Leisure fell 3.7 per cent, dragging the consumer discretionary sector down 0.3 per cent.
On Wall Street the S&P 500 rose 0.8 per cent, recovering more than half its prior-day tumble to a four-month low; the Dow rose 0.4 per cent and the Nasdaq composite 1.4 per cent.
The 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.73 per cent from 4.80 per cent late Tuesday, having been at its highest level since 2007.
ADP reported private employers added 89,000 jobs last month versus the 140,000 economists expected; the US government jobs report is due Friday.
US crude fell $US5.01 to $US84.22 a barrel, its worst drop in just over a year, while Brent lost $US5.11 to $US85.81.
The Fed has raised its main rate to the highest since 2001 and signalled it may keep rates higher next year; its inflation target is 2 per cent.
Kevin McCarthy was ousted as House speaker; US government funding runs until November 17, and Goldman Sachs economists say the leadership vacuum raises the odds of a shutdown.
IG Australia analyst Tony Sycamore said iron ore miners were held back by concerns about China's economy ahead of China's consumer price report next week.
Australian Retailers Association chief Paul Zahra said Christmas spending will be more conservative than last year, with shoppers cutting back on hospitality, home goods and clothes.
